text: This closing lab builds one real agent using everything this chapter covered. A support and ops agent: unstructured documents — troubleshooting guides, past incident write-ups — searched with Cortex Search, structured tables — ticket volumes, SLA breaches, order data — queried in natural language with Cortex Analyst, combined into one Cortex Agent that picks the right tool per question, the same orchestration pattern you evaluated back in Lesson 69's real supply-chain example.

Before building anything, check the AI Readiness Score on the tables you're about to expose. Low semantic view coverage on your ticket or order tables is a signal to build a proper Semantic View first — real primary keys, relationships, metric definitions — rather than pointing Cortex Analyst at raw, undocumented tables and hoping the natural-language layer compensates for missing structure.

Governance gets wired in alongside the tools, not bolted on after the agent already works. Agent Identity confirms this agent shows up correctly as CORTEX_AGENT in QUERY_HISTORY. Masking and row access policies on any PII column key off IS_AGENT_ACTIVATED, even for a role that would otherwise see it unmasked. AI Guardrails protects against prompt injection hidden in the ticket descriptions and documents Cortex Search indexes. And an approval gate sits in front of anything state-modifying — closing a ticket, updating an order — whether that's the built-in permission_policy or an application-layer equivalent you build yourself.

Before calling it done, write five to ten ground-truth question-answer pairs covering both tools and run them through Cortex Agent Evaluation. Check tool_selection_accuracy specifically — a low score there means the agent is reaching for the wrong tool before it even gets to answering, which no amount of prompt tuning on the final response will fix.

That's the full course — seventy-six lessons, seventeen chapters, from your very first virtual warehouse in Lesson 1 to a Cortex Agent you've built, evaluated, and governed end to end. Storage, compute, loading, transformation, modeling, semi-structured data, streams and tasks, security, performance, cost, Power BI, the modern data stack, Cortex AI, and now AI governance. You have a current, production-minded picture of Snowflake — not just the syntax, but the judgment calls around it.
